question: How do the portfolio's valuations compare with public peers?
html:
Portfolio valuations versus public peers

The context has no BSP portfolio marks and no public-peer EV/EBITDA multiples, so a direct valuation comparison cannot be made. What it does support is a comparison of operating economics against 31 public peers, plus private deal multiples that show where a quality premium could sit.

What the data covers

  • Public peers: The peer set reports growth, margins and revenue per employee. It does not report trading multiples (Public comparables, Sep 24, 2026).
  • Private benchmarks: Banker grids and deal prints are available. Capstone/IMAP puts typical middle-market deals at 6.8x and premium deals at 9.8x (ServiceOS evidence, Oct 6, 2026).
  • Size of the premium: Up to about 3 turns of EBITDA for recurring, visible, tech-enabled earnings. Technology itself can claim only about 0.5-2.5 turns of that (ServiceOS evidence).

Company-by-company view

Punctual ProsResidential peers: 14.4% median operating margin, 15.1% EBITDA margin. Residential-only demand is closer to low single digits.PKF puts project-heavy firms at 5-6x and repeatable-service firms at 10x+. Champions sold at about 18.5x and Sila at about 17x (press estimates).1.0-2.5

How to read this

  • Scale drives the top prints. The 17-18.5x roll-up deals reflect scale, density and M&A runway, not technology alone. Their terms were not disclosed by the sponsors (ServiceOS evidence).
  • Peer EBITDA is not adjusted. Public-peer EBITDA is operating income plus D&A, not company-defined Adjusted EBITDA. Impairments depress some latest-year margins (Public comparables).
  • Agent value is assumed, not proven. The AI-agent value of about $12.7M a year (est.) rests on labelled assumptions, not company data (Portfolio AI-agent plan).

Data needed to answer properly

  • Current BSP marks and LTM Adjusted EBITDA for each portfolio company.
  • EV/EBITDA for the 31 public peers, on a consistent definition.
  • The Fair Harbor premium range, which is truncated in the ServiceOS evidence.

Next actions

  1. Pull peer EV/EBITDA for the 31 tickers and reconcile it to the Public comparables EBITDA definition.
  2. Map each portfolio company's latest mark to the relevant banker grid: PKF for Punctual Pros and CET, Aventis for Frontline.
  3. Recover the Fair Harbor range from the full ServiceOS evidence file.
  4. Replace the analyst volume assumptions in the agent plan with system-of-record counts before using its value in exit cases.

# Portfolio valuations versus public peers

The context has no BSP portfolio marks and no public-peer EV/EBITDA multiples, so a direct valuation comparison cannot be made. What it does support is a comparison of operating economics against 31 public peers, plus private deal multiples that show where a quality premium could sit.

## What the data covers

- **Public peers:** The peer set reports growth, margins and revenue per employee. It does not report trading multiples (Public comparables, Sep 24, 2026).
- **Private benchmarks:** Banker grids and deal prints are available. Capstone/IMAP puts typical middle-market deals at 6.8x and premium deals at 9.8x (ServiceOS evidence, Oct 6, 2026).
- **Size of the premium:** Up to about 3 turns of EBITDA for recurring, visible, tech-enabled earnings. Technology itself can claim only about 0.5-2.5 turns of that (ServiceOS evidence).

## Company-by-company view

| Portfolio company | Public-peer economics | Private multiple evidence | Premium est. (turns) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Punctual Pros | Residential peers: 14.4% median operating margin, 15.1% EBITDA margin. Residential-only demand is closer to low single digits. | PKF puts project-heavy firms at 5-6x and repeatable-service firms at 10x+. Champions sold at about 18.5x and Sila at about 17x (press estimates). | 1.0-2.5 |
| CET | Electrical/MEP revenue grew 16.8% a year; commercial electrical median operating margin is 6.4%. | PKF grid; electrical M&A slowed to 99 deals in 2025. | 0.5-1.5 |
| Frontline | Onshore professional services earn 3-9% margins (CBIZ: $290k revenue per employee). | Aventis MSP curve runs 5.2x to 11.2x; entry was about 12-15x (est.). | 0.5-1.5 |
| Thomas Scientific | No disclosed multiple premium from Avantor or Grainger. | Capital structure dominates the exit. | 0.5-1.0 |
| BPI | Agency median growth is +0.3%. | PPHC floor is about 8.4x; estimated sponsor exit is 10-13x. | 0.5-2.0 |
| Fair Harbor | Not in context. | Not in context. | Not in context. |

Sources: Public comparables; ServiceOS evidence.

## How to read this

- **Scale drives the top prints.** The 17-18.5x roll-up deals reflect scale, density and M&A runway, not technology alone. Their terms were not disclosed by the sponsors (ServiceOS evidence).
- **Peer EBITDA is not adjusted.** Public-peer EBITDA is operating income plus D&A, not company-defined Adjusted EBITDA. Impairments depress some latest-year margins (Public comparables).
- **Agent value is assumed, not proven.** The AI-agent value of about $12.7M a year (est.) rests on labelled assumptions, not company data (Portfolio AI-agent plan).

## Data needed to answer properly

- Current BSP marks and LTM Adjusted EBITDA for each portfolio company.
- EV/EBITDA for the 31 public peers, on a consistent definition.
- The Fair Harbor premium range, which is truncated in the ServiceOS evidence.

## Next actions

1. Pull peer EV/EBITDA for the 31 tickers and reconcile it to the Public comparables EBITDA definition.
2. Map each portfolio company's latest mark to the relevant banker grid: PKF for Punctual Pros and CET, Aventis for Frontline.
3. Recover the Fair Harbor range from the full ServiceOS evidence file.
4. Replace the analyst volume assumptions in the agent plan with system-of-record counts before using its value in exit cases.
